chunks: And from him (Al-Hilli) from Fadala from Aban from Hariz from Hakim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"Nothing from fish is disliked except the Jirith." The resolution in these two reports and what follows their pattern is that it is not disliked with the dislike of prohibition, except this Jirith, although it is disliked with the dislike of recommendation and preference. And what we preceded from the reports, even if some of them contained the wording of prohibition, such as the hadith of Ibn Fadl and others, is to be interpreted according to this type of prohibition which we preceded, and that which indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.الْجِرِّيثُ: Jirith, a specific type of fish considered disliked or prohibited by some interpretations
key_terms.كَرَاهِيَةَ النَّدْبِ: Dislike of recommendation (a lesser degree of dislike, where avoiding is preferred)
key_terms.كَرَاهِيَةَ الْحَظْرِ: Dislike of prohibition (resembling haram but not strictly forbidden)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating all types of fish in Shia jurisprudence and what is the exception?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the 'Jirith' (often identified as the sturgeon or a scaleless fish) is not strictly prohibited (haram) but rather disliked (makruh tanzih), reconciling reports that use stronger language of prohibition by interpreting them as referring to this specific level of dislike. This ruling highlights the Shia principle of distinguishing between absolute prohibition and recommended avoidance in dietary laws, emphasizing that most fish are permissible unless explicitly excluded. The context reflects the scholarly effort to harmonize seemingly contradictory hadiths by understanding the nuanced levels of 'karamah' (dislike) in Islamic law.
